Segregation. From the Reconstruction era through the Civil Rights Movement, segregation was the systematic separation of people by race in American society, enforced through both law and custom. It took two forms. De jure segregation was enforced by law through Jim Crow laws, which mandated separate public facilities, schools, and transportation for Black and white Americans. De facto segregation operated through residential discrimination, economic barriers, and social custom, particularly in northern states, without explicit legal mandate. The doctrine of "separate but equal" was established by the Supreme Court in the 1896 Plessy v. Ferguson decision, which upheld segregation as constitutional. In practice, however, separate meant unequal. Black schools received only a fraction of white schools' funding, and facilities were vastly inferior. Segregation permeated American life. Water fountains, restaurants, hospitals, theaters, prisons, and even cemeteries maintained racial separation. The Civil Rights Movement of the nineteen-fifties and sixties directly challenged segregation through sit-ins, freedom rides, and mass demonstrations, making it a defining moral issue for the nation. Brown v. Board of Education in 1954 declared school segregation unconstitutional, though implementation faced massive resistance in the South. This Supreme Court decision represented the culmination of the movement's efforts to dismantle the legal framework that had legitimized racial apartheid for nearly six decades.
